How Do I Protect My Kids' College Plans If I Die Early?

A few simple steps can keep college funding on track even if the unexpected happens.

By Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent (NPN 21370662) · October 2026

Most parents think about college savings in terms of contributions and growth. Fewer think about what happens to the plan if a parent dies before the goal is reached. A solid plan includes protection for the plan itself. Here is a practical approach, in simple steps. Cover the parents first. If you are also thinking about a small policy on the child, see children's life insurance.

Important: this article is educational, not personalized advice. Annuities and life insurance guarantees depend on the issuing company's claims-paying ability, can carry surrender charges and fees, and are not bank products or investments. Speak with a licensed professional and your tax advisor before moving money.

Start with the risk

If a working parent dies, the family loses income and may lose the ability to keep making college contributions. At the same time, the surviving parent may face higher costs, such as childcare, and the need to replace the missing income. College funding is often one of the first goals to suffer. Protection means making sure the money and the plan survive.

Step 1: Get the right amount of life insurance

Term life insurance is built to cover a set number of years, such as the years when your children depend on you. When sizing coverage, include:

  • Income replacement for the years until the youngest child is independent.
  • College costs you want to fund.
  • Debts such as the mortgage.
  • Childcare and household replacement costs if a stay-at-home parent dies.

See how much life insurance you need for a method. Matching the term length to when your youngest will finish college is a common approach.

Step 2: Keep savings accounts in order

  • Name a successor owner on your 529 plan so the account continues smoothly if you die. Check the plan's rules.
  • Keep records of account numbers, login information, and contact details in a place your spouse or trusted person can find.
  • Review beneficiaries on all accounts, including retirement accounts and life insurance.

A 529 and life insurance do different jobs. See life insurance vs. 529.

Do not name a minor child as the direct beneficiary of life insurance proceeds without legal advice. Minors cannot manage money, and a court-supervised arrangement may result. A trust or custodian arrangement is often safer.

Step 3: Consider a trust

A trust can hold life insurance proceeds and direct how they are used, for example for education costs, at specific ages. It can also name a trustee you trust to manage the money. An estate attorney can advise on whether a trust fits your situation and your state's laws.

Step 4: Name guardians and put documents in place

If both parents die, a will naming guardians for minor children is essential. A will, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives are basic documents. Review them after life events such as a new child or a move.

Step 5: Consider disability too

A parent is more likely to become disabled than to die during working years. If your income stopped due to disability, college funding would be at risk too. Disability insurance can protect income. See our disability insurance page.

Step 6: Keep the plan simple and written

Write down the steps: where policies are, which accounts fund college, who the successor owner is, and who to call. Share it with your spouse and a trusted person. A simple plan that is known and findable beats a perfect plan nobody can locate.

A sample action list

  1. Review your life insurance amount and term length.
  2. Apply for additional term coverage if needed.
  3. Name successor owners and update beneficiaries.
  4. Meet with an estate attorney about a will and trust.
  5. Consider disability coverage.
  6. Store documents securely and tell your family.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming employer life insurance is enough.
  • Not naming a successor owner on a 529.
  • Leaving beneficiary forms outdated.
  • Naming a minor directly as beneficiary.
  • Buying a policy that expires before the youngest child finishes college.

Make the plan visible

Even good arrangements can fail if no one knows about them. After you set up insurance, accounts, and legal documents, write a short summary that lists each item, where the documents are, and who to call. Share it with your spouse or a trusted person, and update it each year. A few minutes of organization now can spare your family confusion and delay later.

Review every few years

Children grow, incomes change, and college cost estimates move. Revisit your life insurance amount, your savings, and your documents every few years and after major life events such as a new baby, a move, a career change, or a divorce. Small updates keep the plan matched to your real situation.

Common questions

Protect College Plans FAQ

What kind of life insurance protects college plans?
Many families use term life insurance sized to cover the years their children will need support. Your needs and budget decide the type and the amount.
Should I name my child as a beneficiary?
Naming a minor child directly can create legal complications. Many families use a trust or name a custodian so the money is managed properly. Ask an attorney.
What happens to a 529 plan if the account owner dies?
Most 529 plans allow a successor owner to be named so the account continues, but you must name one, so check your plan's rules.
